about: The machine-readable H3 prompt contract. Read this before auditing, changing, or adding a prompt: it is the one place that states what the output must look like per mode, what vocabulary is legal, what blocks each system prompt carries and in what order, and which guide line each of those comes from. test/contract.test.ts binds every field here to the implementation, so a disagreement is a build failure rather than a stale document.
notWrittenByHand: Nothing here is generated. It is written independently of the code on purpose -- a spec derived from the implementation cannot contradict it, and therefore cannot catch it being wrong. Hand-written is not the same as unchecked, and the distinction matters most exactly where a long vocabulary would otherwise rot: every leaf carries `binds`, so `vocabulary.cameraTypes.values` is compared to the `CAMERA_TYPES` export rather than trusted as a transcription. The hand copy is what lets the spec contradict the code; the binding is what stops it drifting silently. Neither alone would do. This has now paid off once, concretely, which is worth recording because the argument had been abstract: `diagnostics.codes.DIALOGUE_BAD_TERMINAL` read "complete statements end . ? or !", carrying ref 5.4's scope, while the rule in speech.ts demanded a terminal on every line it examined and said so in its own message. The two artifacts disagreed for as long as both existed, the suite was green throughout, and the disagreement was only visible because the spec had not been derived from the code. A generated spec would have restated the implementation's wider rule and agreed with it perfectly.

sources.title: Video Prompt Writing Guide (T2VA / I2VA / FL2VA / L2VA)
sources.note: The hash is checked. A guide revision should be a deliberate, visible event: replace the file, update the hash, and let the golden tests report everything the revision changed.

sources.title: Full-Reference Mode Rewrite Output Format Guide

I2VA.alignment: For the target video, at 0.00 seconds into the target video, <Picture 1> (from [Shot 1]) is fully referenced.

FL2VA.alignment: How the reference pictures align with the target video — Picture 1 (from Shot 1) aligns with the 0.00-second mark of the target video; Picture 2 (from Shot {N}) aligns with the {S.SS}-second mark of the target video.
FL2VA.alignmentNote: Bare. This one line uses Picture 1 and Shot 1 without angle or square brackets, unlike every other citation in the format. The guide's own worked example does, and a fixture proves it.

L2VA.alignment: How the reference pictures align with the target video — <Picture 1> (from [Shot {N}]) aligns with the {S.SS}-second mark of the target video.

shotHeader.note: The cut phrasing itself is prose inside the beat, not part of the header. The guide asks for it as natural language in the sentence.

modes.note: Base 1 names the first four; Ref2VA is the full-reference mode the second guide covers. It was a bare array with no citation while every entry beside it carried one -- the same shape as the two entries an outside audit marked house, caught by the check that now enforces the pattern.

specialCuts.note: Only when the user explicitly asks.

form.unbound: A schematic the spec writes to summarise base 4.4, not a string any guide contains. The guide states the rule in prose and shows filled instances; the delimiters beside this are bound by render.

sceneTrans.note: Both sides of a line that crosses a cut.

cutoff.note: Speech truncated by the end of the video; final beat only.

voiceoverPhrase.note: Exact phrase, followed by a statement that the lips remain closed.

speakerIds.note: Numbered by the order of actual vocal events; never renumbered; never written in retention_analysis (ref 5.4).

onScreenText.quoting: English double quotation marks, verbatim, untranslated

quoting.unbound: A rule about how a string is written, not a string. base 4.5 is the claim; visibleTextQuoted in validate/rules/speech.ts is what enforces it, and it has its own controls.

mediaKinds.note: House partition of reference assets. Neither guide enumerates media kinds; it exists so a slot can be typed.

slotCeilings.note: Not in either guide -- neither states any limit on reference assets. A platform limit carried without a guide citation.

exemptions: video editing: the description scales with the complexity of the source video and is not held to this range
dialogue-dense material: fitting the complete spoken timeline outranks the count
refDetailWords.alsoInTheSameSentence: A single shot does not automatically justify a shorter description; distribute detail across multiple shots according to their information load. Carried by the planner, and recorded here so the spec states the whole clause group rather than the parts that happened to be contested.
refDetailWords.unresolved: Task types combine (ref 3: joined with ' + ', and its own worked example is [video editing + reference generation + audio reuse]). ref 5.2 does not say which clause governs a prefix naming video editing alongside a generation type. Left unresolved here on purpose rather than decided in either direction; the planner is told only not to pad toward the range to satisfy it, since padding is the failure mode either answer would rule out. A guide revision that resolves it is a visible event -- the guide files are hash-checked in sources above.
refDetailWords.note: The scope is part of the rule. Stating the bare range overstates the guide, which is how the planner came to apply it to video-editing jobs.

appliesTo.unbound: A paraphrase of ref 5.2's scoping sentence, not a literal from it. The guide citation is the only binding available; the range beside it is bound by export.

exemptions.unbound: Paraphrases of ref 5.2's own carve-outs. Recorded because a number without its scope is a misquotation, and unbound because no literal in the guide matches this wording.

slotRoles.note: The 19 jobs a reference asset can be given. Neither guide enumerates roles; this is the house partition that decides which label kind a slot gets and whether it earns a standalone definition line, so it is load-bearing rather than descriptive.

frameAnchorRoles.note: Which roles make an image a concrete frame anchor, and therefore earn it a standalone <Picture N> entry. Derived from ref 2.2's distinction between an image used as a frame and one used to define a character or style, but the partition itself is ours.

subjectContentRoles.note: Roles whose content is cited inside a <Subject N> rather than getting a line of its own. The complement of the frame anchors, same provenance.

videoStructureRoles.note: Which roles make a video a whole-video relationship and so earn a standalone <Video N>. Ref 2.3 says <Video N> is reserved for editing, continuation and structural reference; the role names implementing that are ours.

audioRoles.note: Which roles give a soundtrack a job, and so create an <Audio N> for a video slot. Ref 2.5 says an ordinary reference video does not create one merely by containing sound; deciding when it does is ours.

continuityPhrases.note: The four phrasings the guide offers for audio carrying across a cut. Offered to the planner rather than enforced: the guide lists them as options, so a validator matching on them would fire on legitimate prose that said it differently.
values: continues uninterrupted into the next shot
carries over from the previous shot

dialogueAllowedPunctuation.note: Scoped, like the rule that uses it, to dialogue the user did not supply. Base 4.4 preserves supplied punctuation verbatim.

dialoguePlaceholder.note: <d/> marks where a spoken line is spliced into prose. A house token in no guide, written by the planner and consumed by the serializer, so it never reaches H3 -- except when a beat carries it with no dialogue, which the validator reports as DIALOGUE_PLACEHOLDER_ORPHAN.

planner.note: Blocks are joined in this order. Anything marked conditional is absent when its input is absent. Adding a block means adding it here first; the conformance test fails otherwise.

blocks.heading: # How to write
blocks.note: Observable-only description, one action at a time, continuity from beat to beat. Neither guide states any of it; base 4.1 says every detail should correspond to something visible or audible, and this is the house reading of what that asks a writer to do.
blocks.noAnchor: Craft prose with no field name, literal or rendered shape in it. Anchoring a sentence here would make this file a change detector for wording, which is the failure test/creative-integration.test.ts already had once.

blocks.heading: # What the frame can show
blocks.note: Four consequences of base 4.1 that # How to write leaves implicit: absence cannot be rendered so a missing thing is written as its visible evidence; count and position beat adjectives; every property has to be present in one frame; left and right are fixed as the camera sees them. Deliberately narrower than it could be. A fifth rule banning relational placement -- beside, behind her, nearby -- was dropped because the guides' worked examples use it: 'sitting beside <Subject 3> on the sofa' (ref) and 'a closed black umbrella beside a silver bicycle' (base FL2VA). Only the left/right half survives that check, and it survives because no worked example uses body-relative left or right at all.
blocks.noAnchor: Same shape as # How to write: four consequences of base 4.1 stated as prose. The negation half also reaches the patch prompt, where it is likewise unanchorable.

blocks.heading: # Recognisable people
blocks.note: Not in either guide. From the Sora prompt architecture and the original engine's own fragment. Carve-out: dialogue text and on-screen text are reproduced verbatim regardless. Neither guide mentions public figures. From the Sora prompt architecture and the original engine's fragment. Carve-out: dialogue text and on-screen text are reproduced verbatim regardless.
blocks.noAnchor: A prohibition stated in prose. Its only field-shaped token, `dialogue`, is shared with # Speech and so does not tell the two blocks apart -- an anchor that matches a neighbouring block would pass while pointing at the wrong text.

blocks.heading: # Camera
blocks.note: CAMERA_TYPES is an annotation vocabulary, not a filter on prose, and the difference is the first invariant. base 4.3's table is a set of motion concepts and base-en:117 immediately tells you to render them "as a natural English action within the shot, rather than stacked as separate labels" -- which is what the prose does, unconstrained. The closed set is compared only to `shots[].camera.type`, in `cameraTypeValid`, which returns early on a null annotation; `CAMERA_TYPES` is imported by that one rule and by nothing else in validate/ or serialize/. So a motion the table cannot name -- a focus pull, as in MiniMax's own fl2va reproducible payload -- is written freely in the prose with no annotation, and validates clean. Recorded because the closed set reads from outside like a restriction on what may be described, and an audit that assumed so would conclude this build rejects the vendor's own requests. It does not: all five worked examples in test/fixtures produce zero diagnostics. What would be true is the general form -- closed-set enforcement cannot be pointed at ingested prose, so if vendor payloads or an outside corpus were ever taken as fixtures the annotation would have to be extracted rather than the prose matched.

blocks.heading: # Shots and beats
blocks.note: The cut vocabulary and the no-timestamp-on-Shot-1 rule are the guide's. 'Cut only to reveal genuinely new subject, space, state, viewpoint or time' restates base 4.2's preference; the beat structure around it is house.

blocks.heading: # Speech
blocks.note: Carries the continuity fields the planner schema requires -- crossesCut, cutoff, <scenetrans>, <cutoff> and the four phrasings of base 4.4 -- which no prompt named until a review found that a model doing the right thing produced an unclearable SCENETRANS_UNPAIRED. The punctuation instruction is scoped to lines the planner writes: base 4.4 preserves supplied words verbatim, and rewriting one makes the document stop recognising it as the user's. Also carries addressing -- who a line is spoken to. base 4.4 STATES the slot: "Place the speaker's identifying phrase, ID, action, and delivery outside `<d>`", and an addressee is reached through that action. ref 5.4 SHOWS the one worked instance either guide contains -- `<Subject 2> (S1) turns toward the woman and says, <d>[English] ...</d>` -- which is why an addressee is named by visible description or subject label and never by a speaker id: a listener who does not speak has no `(Sx)`, and inventing one creates a vocal source the clip then has to fill. The slot is the guide's; the emphasis is house, because one instance across both guides is not evidence a model follows it reliably. Also carries sung lines, which had no path at all: the block forbade naming a vocal act without supplying its words -- sings included -- and then never said how sung words are supplied. ref 5.1 STATES the answer, "Write dialogue and lyrics as `<d>[Language] ...</d>`", and base 4.4 already treats lyrics as dialogue where one crosses a cut. So a sung line is a dialogue line, the singer takes an id like any other voice, and there is no separate lyrics tag. The release declares a lyrics token pair that neither guide names; the prompt closes that door without naming the tokens, since naming a string is how a model learns it exists. The claim is scoped to the guides for the same reason a guide number carries its scope -- "there is no separate tag for lyrics" is false about the release, while "neither guide names one" is true and is the thing a writer needs. That distinction is load-bearing rather than pedantic: the pair is emitted deliberately in marker experiments elsewhere, so a flat ban would forbid work that is actually being done, and only the scoped form is correct under both readings.

blocks.heading: # Style
blocks.note: Says only that style names the medium and finish. Where it is rendered is contract-specific and lives in the mode blocks: base opens Shot 1 with it as a clause (base 4.1), Ref2VA states it in one or two sentences before [Shot 1] (ref 5.2). The core stated the base shape for every mode until a review found it contradicted the Ref2VA golden fixture.

blocks.heading: # Audio
blocks.note: Wholly 4.6 and 4.7: the sentence ranges, the N/A option, and the condition that governs it. This block previously carried a house lean -- default to N/A unless music was asked for -- recorded in notInTheGuides as music-default, and it has been reverted. The reason is the kind of rule 4.7 states rather than the evidence tally: "Use N/A when there is no non-diegetic music" is a test applied to the scene in front of you, so a default answers it unconditionally and every clip then asserts it is unscored whether or not anything evaluated that. Both directions assert something, which is why neither is a safe default and the guide refuses to have one. The corroboration, which is not the argument: across the guides' worked examples and the three reproducible API payloads MiniMax ships, vendor practice is 2 of 8 toward N/A. Do not re-adopt the lean, and note that a prompt corpus leaning far harder on N/A exists outside this repo and is not a validated source for it.

blocks.heading: # Active mode:
blocks.note: One per mode; the heading carries the mode name. One block per mode. The keyframe semantics are base 3.1-3.3 and the full-reference differences are ref 5.2; the glitch-mark affordances appended to it are house and marked in notInTheGuides. The Ref2VA block also carries ref 5.4's two rules for reused words, which nothing stated before it: words carried across from an audio asset or reperformed on request are reproduced exactly in their original language with `[unclear]` for spans that cannot be made out, and an asset referenced only for timbre, rhythm, emotion or delivery does not carry its words across at all. `[unclear]` is not asserted here because this entry's anchors have to hold for whichever mode block is present, and the marker is Ref2VA's alone; it is asserted against a Ref2VA prompt in test/contract.test.ts instead. One scoping is ours rather than the guide's: an audio slot reaches the planner as a written description and never as audio, so the unintelligible span the guide has in mind is, here, any span the description does not supply -- which is what makes the marker the honest output rather than an invented line.

blocks.heading: # What your plan becomes
blocks.note: MiniMax's worked example for the active mode, quoted whole. The prompt was rules with no instance of the artifact they describe, and both guides teach this format mostly by worked example -- four Cases in base 5, one complete example in ref 7. The vendor's five rather than a house-authored set because these are what H3 was trained near, which outranks grading conformant. One ships per call, since the mode selects it. The framing around it is load-bearing rather than decorative: the model returns a plan and this is the output, so an example presented without that distinction invites finished prompt text back and a schema failure. `quotesOutput` exempts this block from anchor uniqueness, and that flag is why it is a separate block rather than an appendix to the mode block -- a block quoting a real prompt contains the camera phrasing, the dialogue tags and the field labels that other blocks anchor on, so it would collide with them by construction and every future anchor would have to be chosen to avoid five worked examples. Its own anchors are still asserted present by the per-block check above.

blocks.heading: # Style direction
blocks.note: From CreativeModeRecord.selection. Absent when no pack resolves. Derived from a CreativeModeRecord. Injects pack directives that no guide mentions; the packs are in notInTheGuides.
blocks.noAnchor: Derived from a CreativeModeRecord, so the text is pack data rather than prompt prose. That the planner and patch prompts derive the same directive from the same record is asserted in test/creative-integration.test.ts.

blocks.heading: # Glitch marks
blocks.note: From CreativeModeRecord.glitch. The planner appends a mode-specific affordance note; the patch prompt does not, because it has no mode. Derived from a CreativeModeRecord's glitch half. Entirely house; it defers to base 4.5 for how a mark is written, rather than restating it.
blocks.noAnchor: Derived, like # Style direction, and asserted in the same place.

blocks.heading: # Supplied facts
blocks.note: Last on purpose, so the facts have the final word. Computed values handed to the model as fact -- duration, latest legal cut, label assignments, budgets -- so it never derives arithmetic. The values trace to the guides; presenting them this way does not.
asserts: Spoken-word budget for the whole clip, as a ceiling and not a target:

blocks.heading: # Rules
blocks.note: How a surgical edit behaves: change only what was asked, keep register, preserve continuity. No guide describes editing an existing prompt. Carries the negation half of the planner's # What the frame can show, and only that half: the rule is asymmetric, since an edit that may write 'no other people' reintroduces exactly what the planner was stopped from writing. The rest of that block is composition guidance a surgical edit has no use for. Tells the edit that an N/A in `music` is a judgement and not a gap, for the same asymmetry: `music` is on PATCHABLE_LEAVES, so an edit is otherwise free to invent a score over a silence the planner decided on per scene. This outlived the music-default lean it was introduced alongside -- it is ordinary edit conservatism over a field whose legitimate value looks like an empty one, and it does not restore a default.

blocks.heading: # When you should refuse
blocks.note: Structural changes a patch cannot express are declined rather than approximated. House.

blocks.heading: # Active style
blocks.note: Same derivation as the planner's # Style direction, framed as preservation.
blocks.noAnchor: A one-sentence wrapper around a derived directive; the wrapper names no field and the directive is pack data, asserted in test/creative-integration.test.ts.

blocks.heading: # Active glitch marks
blocks.note: Same derivation as the planner's # Glitch marks, framed as preservation, and with no mode note because a patch has no mode.

patch.parity: Both prompts derive the style and glitch blocks from the same record through the same function, so an edit cannot drift from what the document was written under. test/creative-integration.test.ts asserts the derived text is identical on both sides.

invariants.statement: The planner writes the sentences; the serializer assembles structure around them and never expands an enum into a sentence.
invariants.enforcedBy: review, and the absence of any enum-to-prose path in src/core/serialize

invariants.statement: serialize(doc, ctx) is total and deterministic. Nothing hand-edits prompt text.
src/core has no React, DOM, network, SDK or idb.
A diagnostic means the document is provably malformed. There is no warning severity.
Every diagnostic code has a fixture that makes it fire.
A creative selection and a wildcard roll travel as records; their text is derived at the point of use.
The five golden fixtures are the guides' worked examples, byte for byte.
Stored ids this build does not know resolve to nothing rather than failing to load.
A patch never writes a value H3DocumentSchema rejects for that leaf.

diagnostics.note: Every code the validator can emit, with what makes it legitimate. Guide-derived codes cite a section; house codes say so. test/validate.test.ts proves each one can fire; the conformance test proves this list matches the codes the rules actually emit. What no check reaches, stated because it has already been escaped through: these descriptions are prose about a condition, and nothing compares them to the condition. The bindings cover a code's existence and its provenance -- the set matches what the rules emit, and every reason cites a guide section or declares itself house -- so DIALOGUE_BAD_TERMINAL could describe ref 5.4's "complete statements" while the rule demanded a terminal on every line, and did, with the suite green. No check is offered for it and the reason is not that an instance is lacking; it is that the property is undecidable. Whether a sentence describes a boolean expression is not mechanically answerable, there is no allowlist here whose growth is the dangerous direction, and a proxy over the message text would fail on every legitimate rewording -- the brittleness this spec has already been bitten by twice. One narrow version was weighed and rejected, recorded here so the argument does not run again: assert that a description mentions the concept its branch tests -- that DIALOGUE_BAD_TERMINAL says "complete" where the code branches on incompleteness. It would have caught this exact instance, which is what makes it tempting. It loses because it is a wording proxy wearing an identifier costume: it passes only while someone happens to have chosen that word, so a description reading "a finished utterance" fails it while being perfectly correct, and the first legitimate rewrite turns it red for nothing. That is the same failure as the wording proxies this spec has already had to widen twice. The control that exists is a person reading the description beside the rule when either changes, and this note is where they are told to.

codes.NO_SHOTS: house: a document with no shots renders nothing
codes.DURATION_NOT_POSITIVE: house: duration drives every derived timestamp
codes.MODE_SLOT_MISMATCH: house: base 1 describes what each mode is, not how many references it takes. The cardinalities the rule enforces -- exactly one first-frame image for I2VA, exactly two for FL2VA, no other media -- appear nowhere in either guide. Defensible policy, not contract.
codes.SHOT_1_HAS_TIMESTAMP: base 4.2: the first shot carries no timestamp
codes.CUT_OUTSIDE_DURATION: base 4.2: cuts fall within the video duration
codes.SHOT_NO_BEATS: house: a shot with no prose renders an empty header
codes.FRAME_ROLE_ON_NON_IMAGE: ref 2.2: only images are frame anchors
codes.SLOT_NO_ROLES: house: a slot with no role has no label kind
codes.SLOT_ORDER_NOT_CONTIGUOUS: house: connection order drives label ordinals
codes.SPEAKER_ORDER_WRONG: base 4.4: ids follow the order of actual vocal events
codes.SPEAKER_REF_MISSING_IN_PROSE: base 4.4: the id is written in the prose
codes.DIALOGUE_PLACEHOLDER_ORPHAN: house: a splice point with nothing to splice
codes.DIALOGUE_BAD_TERMINAL: ref 5.4: complete statements end . ? or ! -- scoped to dialogue the user did not supply, since base 4.4 preserves supplied punctuation verbatim, and scoped to complete utterances, which is what `fragment` on the dialogue annotation records. This description had the guide's scope right while the rule did not: the code required a terminal on every line, so a chant or an interjection failed, and nothing compared the two because the spec binds a diagnostic's existence and not its condition. `fragment` joins crossesCut and cutoff in one incompleteness disjunction rather than arriving as a fourth unrelated flag; it is named for completeness and not for delivery, because a sung line can be a complete statement and a spoken interjection is a fragment, so `sung` would leak both ways.
codes.DIALOGUE_DECORATIVE_PUNCT: ref 5.4: no repeated or decorative punctuation -- same scope, and for the same reason
codes.VOICEOVER_PHRASE_MISSING: base 4.4: the exact phrase. The lips-closed clause the same section requires is a prompt instruction, not a check: the guide mandates the statement rather than a wording, so no allowlist can prove its absence
codes.SCENETRANS_UNPAIRED: base 4.4: both sides of a line crossing a cut
codes.CUTOFF_NOT_AT_END: base 4.4: truncation by the end of the video
codes.REF_TASK_TYPE_DUPLICATE: ref 3: do not repeat a type
codes.REF_SUMMARY_NEW_LABEL: ref 3: no new labels in the summary
codes.REF_LABEL_UNDEFINED: ref 2: a cited label is defined
codes.REF_RETENTION_MISSING: ref 4: one line per reference label
codes.REF_RETENTION_MARKER_WRONG_CLASS: ref 4.1 and 4.2: visual and audio markers are different sets
codes.REF_SPEAKER_IN_RETENTION: ref 5.4: do not write (Sx) in retention_analysis

notInTheGuides.note: Everything the compiler does that no guide asks for. An audit should be able to tell contract from house style at a glance.

items.why: Naming a public figure pulls the frame toward a likeness. From the Sora prompt architecture.
Style direction injected into the planner prompt. Never reaches the serializer.
Anomalous tokenizer strings placed as visible on-screen text. Uses the guide's on-screen text rule rather than a new one.

Absence written as visible evidence, count and position over adjectives, every property present in one frame, and left/right fixed to the camera. Unsourced craft, kept only in the part the guides' worked examples do not contradict. The negation rule also reaches the patch prompt, because an edit free to write an absence undoes the planner's half of it.
Content substitution on the idea, before anything is planned. Never touches beat prose or serialized output.
17k+5 at 24fps is a workflow fact, not a guide rule.

2.5 words per second is an estimate, supplied to the planner as advice. Its shape is assumed rather than measured and it is not cited as a finding anywhere. It is now presented to the model as a ceiling rather than a target, with the difference stated: a fast exchange is many turns and few words, so a short total is not a shortfall, and a budget read as a target gets padded toward. That is the same anti-padding instruction the Ref2VA block already carried for ref 5.2's word range, which the base path had gone without.

MS_PER_BEAT, one dominant beat per 2.5 seconds. House judgement. Neither guide contains a density rule, and the comment here attributed one to the guide until an outside audit searched for it. The density is unchanged, deliberately: a scene built to push fast back-and-forth to its limit is an extreme point and cannot retune a default, and the constant is still right for scenes that are not that one. What was added is a floor rather than a new density -- `recommendedBeats` takes the supplied dialogue count and never returns fewer beats than there are lines. That half is structural and not a judgement: a beat carries at most one `dialogue` object, so N lines need N beats before any action beat exists. It raises and never lowers.
SLOT_CEILINGS, 9 images / 3 videos / 3 audio. Neither guide states any limit on reference assets; marked house in the vocabulary block as well.

The only text sent to a model that no prompt builder wrote, and the only place this spec does not describe the string the model receives. When schema enforcement is off -- a per-call choice now, not a property of the backend -- the client appends the serialized JSON Schema to the system prompt after buildPlannerSystemPrompt has returned, and parses the reply defensively. That applies to every provider: heylook always, since neither of its wires can constrain decoding, and Gemini whenever enforceSchema is false. It lands AFTER '# Supplied facts', which prompts.planner.blocks places last so the facts have the final word -- accepted because a format instruction is a different axis from the craft guidance that note is about, and because it must be the last thing read before the model emits. Invisible to test/contract.test.ts, which indexes into the builder's output rather than the sent string; asserted in test/heylook.test.ts instead, and the breakage confirming contract.test.ts stays green while that one goes red was run.
